text: The If Condition activity works exactly like an if statement in any programming language. It evaluates one expression to true or false, and runs a genuinely different set of activities depending on which — any combination of parameters, variables, or another activity's output can feed that expression.

A real example worth remembering: check whether a Lookup activity's row count is actually greater than zero, copy the data if it is, and run a Fail activity with a clear message if it genuinely isn't. Configure the True activities and the False activities separately, and the branch that runs depends entirely on that one expression.

Switch works exactly like a switch statement instead. It evaluates one expression down to a string, then runs whichever case's activities actually match that value — or the default activities, if nothing matches at all. Route a pipeline's behavior based on a region parameter, say, with each case copying data into a different destination.

Three or more distinct outcomes from one single value get genuinely hard to read as nested If Conditions — an if inside the false branch of another if, inside another. Switch expresses that exact same logic flatter and far more legibly. Reach for If Condition when there are truly only two paths; reach for Switch the moment there are three or more, up to a real maximum of twenty-five cases. Next: the ForEach activity — repeating a set of activities once for every single item in a collection.
